identity.topic: What a Roman legionary's pay would buy across eras
identity.audience: general audience, teens and adults, English
identity.central_question: Was a Roman legionary rich, and in whose money?
identity.unique_angle: one soldier's purse carried through five eras, priced in bread, rent and days of work
identity.tone: dry wit, curious, numbers told straight
identity.emotional_arc: pride, doubt, surprise, a quiet verdict
identity.stakes: the soldier must decide whether to re-enlist
identity.payoff: the purse is worth most in the era nobody guesses
identity.beyond_a_summary: prices converted through wages and bread, not exchange rates, with the arithmetic shown

viewer_takeaway.understand: money is measured in work and food, not coins
viewer_takeaway.feel: sympathy for a man counting his pay
viewer_takeaway.question: what is my pay worth in bread?

jurisdictions.basis: platform in the US; creator assumed in Georgia

rules.requirement: realistic altered or synthetic content is disclosed; fully animated content is not
a real historical person is never shown endorsing, committing a crime or saying an invented quote as fact
no voice imitates a living person without consent
music has a licence record and is never a score or a sound-alike
a number appears on screen with its arithmetic at least once per era

risks.element: Julius Caesar as a drawn caricature paying the soldier
a coin photo from a museum website
risks.evidence: museum page states all rights reserved
risks.rationale: the photograph itself is a protected work; the coin design is ancient but the photo is not
risks.mitigation: draw the coin ourselves from several references
risks.resolved: drawn coin c01 replaces the photo

original_contribution: wage-to-bread conversion argued step by step

creative.mechanism: one purse travels through five eras and is re-priced in bread at each stop
visual_invariants: the purse looks the same in every era

memorable_moments.what: the bread ladder grows beside the coins

avoid_patterns.pattern: a scientist explains in a cave

creative.channel_identity: worlds collide, the drawn universe, Dirkus and Tick

must: every number in the claim map with two sources and a label (established / reasoned / guess)
Caesar's lines are invented and said to be invented; no real quote unless it is one (ER-02)
the narrator's library voice only; no character voice imitates a real person (ER-03)
our drawn universe (UR-22); Caesar as our caricature, never from a photograph or a film actor's face
own or licensed tracks with a licence record; never a film score or a sound-alike (ER-04)
library sounds with a licence record (Q-T16)
the coin-count proof stays on screen long enough to read (ED-10)
no fair-use or 'no infringement intended' text; credits only from verified records (ES-11, ES-12)
